themes.definition: Duties to mark AI outputs in machine-readable form and to label deep fakes and AI-generated text so that the public can tell the content is artificial.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of generative systems must ensure outputs are 'marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated', as far as technically feasible (Art. 50(2), Recital 133), and deployers must disclose deep fakes, more lightly for evident art or satire, and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest (Art. 50(4)); the Commission's guidelines give as an in-scope example an AI-generated message on a meteorological institute's website (per the coder note). The transparency code (EU121) sets the form: an EU icon or equivalent label with 'AI' as its main element, perceivable 'at the latest at the time of first exposure', audible disclaimers for audio, accessible formats under the European Accessibility Act, and attention to audiences of differing literacy, including children; for closed internal professional uses such as staff training, the disclosure may sit in the user interface. Signatories are encouraged to publish what their label means and to provide channels for flagging missing or incorrect labels, and 'will review cases that have been reported in a substantiated manner as mislabelled' and remedy them. Providers keep their own responsibility when relying on third-party marking tools, and give market surveillance authorities documentation and access to their marking and detection solutions on reasoned request. Code measures marked 'will' are mandatory for signatories, but the code states no consequence for breaching them.
themes.holders: Providers of generative AI systems; deployers who generate deep fakes or publish AI-generated text on matters of public interest (which can include public bodies [inference]); EU121 Signatories.
themes.binding: Statutory duties (Art. 50), fineable up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%, and up to EUR 750 000 for Union bodies; recitals use 'should'; Commission guidelines are non-binding interpretation; code measures are 'will' (mandatory for Signatories), 'encouraged' or 'may'; the code states no consequence and says compliance is monitored by market surveillance authorities.
themes.checks: Review of mislabelled content (EU121 Measure 2.3): trigger: a substantiated report; compared against: Art. 50(4) and (5); metric or threshold: not stated; who: the signatory deployer; what happens with the result: remedy without undue delay. Marking (EU121 Measure 1.1): trigger: not stated; compared against: the requirements in Commitment 3; metric: not stated (Recital 133 asks for techniques that are reliable, interoperable, effective and robust, with no thresholds); who: the provider's documented internal testing, reviewable by market surveillance authorities; result: demonstrates compliance.

quotes.quote: shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated

Signatories commit to implement such disclosure through the available EU icon provided in Annex 1 of the Code or through an equivalent icon or label that complies with the design and placement specifications
Signatories will review cases that have been reported in a substantiated manner as mislabelled or incorrectly labelled and take measures to remedy cases of non-compliance with Article 50(4)

obliges deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest to disclose that such text has been artificially generated or manipulated.

themes.theme: Human review and editorial responsibility as the exemption from labelling AI text
themes.definition: The rule that AI-generated text on matters of public interest need not be labelled if it has undergone human review or editorial control and a named person holds editorial responsibility.
themes.what_is_set_out: Art. 50(4) exempts deployers from disclosing AI-generated text published to inform the public where the content 'has undergone a process of human review or editorial control' and 'a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility' (per the coder note; Recital 134). The Commission's Art. 50 guidelines say this person 'must hold the ultimate legal responsibility over the publication of the content, including the human review or editorial control', and that the identity and contact details of the person or function with editorial responsibility 'should be made publicly available on an easily findable location', such as website terms or a colophon, 'To ensure public accountability and trust'. The transparency code (EU121, Commitment 4) commits signatories to publish those contact details where they are not already public. [inference] This is the cell's clearest link between human review of AI outputs and accountability: human review substitutes for disclosure, and the person accountable for it is named publicly. What the review must check, how thoroughly, and how it is recorded are not stated.
themes.holders: Deployers that publish AI-generated or AI-manipulated text on matters of public interest; the natural or legal person, or function, holding editorial responsibility; EU121 Signatories (the holder field excludes some media service providers, but the input text is cut off before saying which).
themes.binding: Statutory exemption (Art. 50(4)); Recital 134 is non-binding; the guidelines are non-binding interpretation ('must hold', 'should be made publicly available'); EU121 is a code commitment. If the conditions are not met, the exemption is lost and disclosure is required, with fines for non-disclosure.
themes.checks: Trigger: before publication of AI-generated or AI-manipulated text on matters of public interest; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated; who: a natural or legal person, or a function, with editorial responsibility; what happens with the result: the text may be published without an AI label, and that person's identity and contact details are published. What the review must examine, how thoroughly, and how it is recorded are not stated.

quotes.quote: AI-generated or manipulated text to the extent it is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest unless the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control
This entails that said person must hold the ultimate legal responsibility over the publication of the content, including the human review or editorial control
the identity and contact details of the legal person, the natural person or the function with editorial responsibility should be made publicly available on an easily findable location

Where not already publicly available, Signatories commit to publish the contact details of the function, the natural persons or the legal person s with editorial responsibility to ensure accountability.

themes.theme: Complaints to regulators, whistleblowing and courts
themes.definition: Routes by which any person, affected party, downstream provider or whistleblower can bring an AI Act infringement before a regulator or a court.
themes.what_is_set_out: Any natural or legal person with grounds to think the AI Act has been infringed may complain to the relevant market surveillance authority, 'without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies' (Art. 85; Recital 170; EU043 para 53; EU_Art50 para 151); complaints are taken into account for market surveillance and, under the Omnibus, can trigger AI Office action. Downstream providers may complain to the AI Office about general-purpose model providers, with duly reasoned complaints (Art. 89(2), Recital 162, EU088). Whistleblowers are protected through Directive 2019/1937 (Art. 87), and the AI Act is added to the directive on representative actions, which the coder reads as opening collective redress [inference]. EU043 adds that the prohibitions have direct effect, so affected parties can seek interim injunctions in national courts, available even before the penalty provisions applied. The transparency code encourages channels for trusted flaggers, researchers, academics and fact-checkers to flag missing or incorrect labels. What a complainant receives in return (a reply, a deadline, an outcome) is not stated in any passage.
themes.holders: Any natural or legal person; affected persons; downstream providers; whistleblowers; individuals and third parties flagging labels; market surveillance authorities, the AI Office and the EDPS (receive complaints); national courts.
themes.binding: Statutory rights (Arts 85, 87, 89(2)); recitals use 'should'; direct effect of the prohibitions is the Commission's interpretation (EU043); the code's flagging channels are only encouraged. Consequences for the operator: possible enforcement action; for the complainant, nothing stated.

quotes.quote: any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the provisions of this Regulation may submit complaints to the relevant market surveillance authority.
prohibitions themselves have direct effect and thus enable affected parties to enforce them in national courts and request interim injunctions against the prohibited practices.
Under Article 89(2) AI Act, downstream providers have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of the AI Act by providers of general-purpose AI model s.

Signatories are encouraged to provide channels that allow individuals or third parties (e.g., trusted flaggers, independent researchers, academics, fact-checkers) to flag missing or incorrect disclosures

themes.theme: Data subject rights against AI models and their outputs
themes.definition: Data protection routes by which individuals can access, correct, erase or object to personal data in AI training data, models and outputs, and what controllers must do in response.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS says EU institutions developing or deploying generative AI 'shall implement and maintain effective procedures' for individuals to exercise their rights, and should sort each request by whether it concerns training data, post-training data, prompts or outputs. Where a request concerns outputs, such as inaccurate personal data generated about someone, the controller 'has to take steps to verify whether the personal data processed are inaccurate' and act, and people can ask for correction whether the error is 'in the training personal dataset or in the output of the AI system'. To answer such requests the controller must find where personal data were used in training and 'assess whether the model, when answering certain prompts, might leak that data'; training datasets should carry metadata, and 'When machine un-learning is not viable, output filtering can be used'. A controller need not erase or alter all models unless the model contains the data or can be used to infer it, and the rights do not apply if the controller shows it cannot identify the individual. The EDPB lists optional measures: an unconditional opt-out before processing, an assured right to object where legitimate interest is relied on, and letting data subjects submit claims of 'personal data regurgitation or memorisation' that controllers can reproduce; data subjects can request deletion, and supervisory authorities may order erasure of their own motion. [inference] This is the cell's most specific treatment of individual AI outputs, but it is limited to personal data.
themes.holders: EUIs and other controllers (must respond); data subjects (right-holders); supervisory authorities (may order erasure).
themes.binding: Statutory rights under the GDPR and EUDPR restated in non-binding guidance ('shall', 'has to', 'must'); some steps are possible measures ('can be used', 'should include'); the EDPB's extra safeguards are optional ('may'). Consequences of failing to respond are mostly not stated.
themes.checks: Output accuracy (EDPS): trigger: a data subject's request about an output; compared against: the accuracy of the personal data; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the controller; what happens with the result: rectification, erasure or output filtering. Leakage (EDPS_AI_risk): trigger: a rights request; compared against: whether the model, 'when answering certain prompts', leaks training data; metric: not stated; who: the controller; result: not stated. Regurgitation claims (EU074): trigger: a data subject's claim; compared against: reproduction of the claimed output; metric: not stated; who: the controller; result: assessment of unlearning techniques.

quotes.quote: The controller has to take steps to verify whether the personal data processed are inaccurate and if the right to rectification is applicable, to take appropriate action.

quotes.location: p.36, s.5.5.1 Risk 1: Incomplete identification o…
quotes.quote: the controller must both identify whether and where personal data are used during the training phase, and assess whether the model, when answering certain prompts, might leak that data when making inferences.
Allowing data subjects to submit claims of personal data regurgitation or memorisation and the circumstances and means by which the claim claim s may be reproduced
When machine un-learning is not viable, output filtering can be used.

themes.definition: Statements that providers, deployers and conformity assessors remain liable under civil liability law for harm.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers testing in real-world conditions are liable under Union and national liability law for damage caused during testing (Art. 60(9)), and sandbox participants 'remain liable' for damage to third parties even though they are exempt from fines when acting in good faith (Art. 57(12)). EU043 says the prohibitions are 'without prejudice to any liability' that providers or deployers may incur for harm under applicable Union or national law, with the conditions set by that law. Notified bodies must hold liability insurance for their conformity assessment work unless the Member State assumes liability or is itself directly responsible. No passage says how a person harmed by a public body's AI tool would bring a claim; the AI Act points to other law.
themes.holders: Providers and prospective providers testing in real-world conditions or in sandboxes; providers and deployers; notified bodies.
themes.binding: Statutory pointers to existing liability law; the insurance duty is statutory (notified-body obligations fineable under Art. 99(4)(f)). The conditions for liability are left to other instruments.

quotes.quote: The provider or prospective provider shall be liable under applicable Union and national liability law for any damage caused in the course of their testing in real world conditions.
Providers and prospective providers participating in the AI regulatory sandbox shall remain liable under applicable Union and national liability law for any damage inflicted on third parties
the prohibitions in the AI Act are without prejudice to any liability that the provider or deployer might incur for the harm caused according to applicable Union or national liability laws.
Notified bodies shall take out appropriate liability insurance for their conformity assessment activities

themes.theme: Administrative fines and penalties on operators
themes.definition: The fine tiers, penalty rules and weighing factors by which operators answer for AI Act breaches.
themes.what_is_set_out: Member States must set 'effective, proportionate and dissuasive' penalties, which may include warnings and non-monetary measures, for infringements by operators (Art. 99(1), Recitals 168 and 179; the Omnibus extends this to 'any infringement'). Fines reach EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices; EUR 15 000 000 or 3% for breaches of the duties of providers, authorised representatives, importers, distributors, deployers (Art. 26), notified bodies and the Art. 50 transparency rules; and EUR 7 500 000 or 1% for misleading information to authorities; the Omnibus adds the value-chain duties of Art. 25(2) and (4). Authorities weigh gravity, number affected, intent, cooperation and size (Art. 99(7)), respect ne bis in idem where one practice breaches several provisions, and may enforce the same conduct under other Union law too; adherence to an adequate code may count as mitigation. Misclassifying a system as not high-risk to avoid requirements, or failing to correct it, is fineable (Art. 80(4), (7)); the Commission may fine general-purpose model providers up to 3% or EUR 15 000 000, including for failing to notify; and the Omnibus gives the AI Office fines and periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily turnover per day. Penalties for the prohibitions applied from 2 August 2025, sandbox participants acting in good faith are exempt from fines, and EU043 suggests national laws on police biometric identification include sanctions for formal and substantive breaches.
themes.holders: Operators (providers, authorised representatives, importers, distributors, deployers) and notified bodies (subject to fines); providers of general-purpose AI models; Member States (lay down rules); the Commission and the AI Office (impose fines); competent authorities (set amounts).
themes.binding: Statutory sanctions with upper limits; amounts and procedures for most operators set by Member State rules; recitals use 'should'; EU043's list for national biometric laws is a suggestion; code adherence as mitigation is discretionary ('may').

quotes.quote: Providers and deployers engaging in prohibited AI practices may be fined up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover
Non-compliance with any of the following provisions related to operators or notified bodies, other than those laid down in Articles 5, shall be subject to administrative fines

the AI system was misclassified by the provider as non-high-risk in order to circumvent the application of requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, the provider shall be subject to fines in accordance with Article 99

quotes.location: Art. 1(32), inserting AI Act Art. 75c(5); pp. 31-…
quotes.quote: Those penalty payments shall be effective and proportionate, and, where applicable, shall not exceed 5 % of the average daily income or worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year per day

themes.definition: Whether, and how far, public authorities and EU institutions that provide or deploy AI can themselves be fined or have projects stopped.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act makes deployers' duties fineable, but leaves it to 'Each Member State' to decide 'to what extent administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State' (Art. 99(8)); EU043 repeats this for public bodies as providers and deployers and gives no default. For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, the EDPS may impose fines, capped at EUR 1 500 000 for prohibited practices and EUR 750 000 for other breaches including the Art. 50 transparency duties (Art. 100; EU043; EU_Art50), after giving the body the opportunity to be heard; the fines 'shall not affect the effective operation' of the body fined and go to the EU budget. Inside the European Parliament, the proposed 2024 framework says non-compliance with the risk and impact assessment process 'should lead to the suspension of the AI project', without saying who suspends it. [inference] The financial consequence for a national public body therefore depends on national law, and for a Union body it is capped and shaped so as not to disrupt the body.
themes.holders: Member States (decide); national public authorities and bodies as providers and deployers; Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies; the EDPS (imposes fines on Union bodies); the European Parliament's AI governance (internal suspension).
themes.binding: Statutory (Arts 99(8) and 100); recitals use 'should'; EU043 and EU_Art50 restate; EP2024 is a proposed internal rule ('should'). Default for national public bodies: not stated.
themes.checks: EP2024 suspension: trigger: non-compliance with the assessment process; compared against: the process; metric or threshold: not stated; who: not stated; what happens with the result: suspension of the AI project. Other passages: n/a.

quotes.quote: Each Member State shall lay down rules on to what extent administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State.
The European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of this Regulation.
The fines shall not affect the effective operation of the Union institution, body, office or agency fined.
EU institutions, bodies and agencies that violate the transparency obligations may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000.

absences: All eight starting codes for Accountability appear in this cell: named accountable roles, sign-off, publication, registration, reporting to regulators or boards, audit, complaint and redress routes, and sanctions. Several are thin. Sign-off falls only on providers (declaration of conformity, CE marking, signed test logs); no passage requires a public body, as deployer, to sign off a tool before use, and none names an accountable official inside a public body for a given tool. The Commission's guidelines say individual employees are not deployers, so accountability sits with the organisation; named individuals appear only as the persons who register entries in the EU database, holders of editorial responsibility for AI-generated text, and, as a suggestion for national law, the responsible staff for police biometric identification. Binding audit is limited to notified bodies' audits of providers' quality management systems and AI Office inspections; audit of public bodies' own AI use appears only as ECA commitments and EU043 suggestions. Internal reporting by public bodies to their own boards (AI@EC, EP2024) has no stated frequency, threshold or consequence, and no passage requires a national public body to report on its AI use to a national parliament, ombudsman or audit office. Consequences for public bodies are left to Member States (Art. 99(8)) and, for Union bodies, are capped. Redress for people affected by a wrong AI output in a public service is limited: the right to explanation covers only Annex III high-risk systems with significant effects; complaints go to the market surveillance authority with no stated reply, deadline or outcome; liability is left to other law; and Recital 59 names the difficulty of challenging AI results in court without providing a mechanism. On checking AI outputs, the cell gives no accuracy metric or threshold, nothing on consistency or repeatability, confidence scores, or the recording of prompts, configuration or model versions used in a decision, and does not say which cases must reach a human. The nearest items are the suggested audit of 'accuracy criteria' for police biometric identification, documentation of 'the results of its evaluation' for model providers, the training-summary update on retraining, the EDPS duty to verify inaccurate personal data in outputs, the human-review exemption from labelling AI text, the right to human intervention under the EUDPR, and the ECA's aim to examine the 'quality and reliability' of auditees' algorithms. Publication of public-sector use is incomplete: law enforcement, migration, asylum and border uses are registered in a non-public section, the Commission's internal AI register is not said to be published, and sandbox exit reports are published only by agreement.
cross_cutting: The cell is dominated by the AI Act (EU046) and the Commission's guidance and amendments built on it (EU043, EU_Art50, EU088, EU090, EU121, EU_Omnibus); data protection guidance from the EDPS and EDPB adds a second, controller-based line of accountability, and the JRC, ECA, Commission (AI@EC) and Parliament documents add internal or recommended arrangements. Accountability runs mostly upward and on request: operators keep documentation and answer to market surveillance authorities, the EDPS or the AI Office when asked; national authorities report to the Commission; and the Commission answers to the Parliament and Council. Duties fall chiefly on providers; public bodies appear mainly as deployers, with duties to register their use before deployment, notify the regulator of their fundamental rights impact assessment, inform affected people and workers, explain decisions on request, report serious incidents and cooperate, while the guidance keeps accountability with the organisation rather than individual staff and insists that relying on suppliers, contractors or AI outputs does not shift it. The AI Act and Omnibus passages are statutory and backed by graded fines, but whether national public authorities can be fined is left to each Member State and fines on Union bodies are capped and must not disrupt them; the guidance documents are non-binding, and the internal EU-institution and JRC passages are commitments or recommendations with almost no stated consequence. Routine audit, internal sign-off by public deployers, and redress routes with stated outcomes for people affected by public-sector AI are thin. On checking AI outputs, accountability here is mainly about who must be able to show what to whom: the burden of demonstrating compliance on operators, documentation of testing and evaluation results for supervisors, rights to explanation and human intervention, human editorial review as a substitute for labelling AI text, and data subjects' routes to correct inaccurate outputs. No document in the cell sets a metric, threshold or schedule for checking outputs, and the external checks that exist are triggered by suspicion, complaint or request.
